facts.fact: The World Bank's ID4D diagnostic, from a field assessment of 23-28 June 2014, states that every civil registry office keeps bound paper ledgers, one for births and one for deaths, in which registration is made by hand in two copies, and that Law 37.99 covers only a paper-based register.

The World Bank's ID4D diagnostic (field assessment June 2014) states that births and deaths are entered by hand in paper registers, that birth registration information is not centralised nationally and that the civil register continues to exist in paper ledgers only, about 45 million records in all.

The World Bank's ID4D diagnostic (field assessment June 2014) counts about 2,200 civil registry offices in the country (1,503 principal offices, 1,282 of them rural and 221 urban, and about 700 annexes) plus 69 consular posts, all registering by hand; it adds that no official statistics exist but the majority of the 2,200 are believed to have no connected computer systems.

The World Bank's ID4D diagnostic (field assessment June 2014) states that civil registration is managed by the DGCL, a directorate of the Ministry of Interior, whose small central civil registration office coordinates the commune offices, where the president of the local council is the civil registration officer.

The World Bank's ID4D diagnostic (field assessment June 2014) states that equipping the civil registry offices falls to the municipal councils of the communes, which use their own budgets at their discretion; the annual budget for civil registration was not disclosed to the team.

systems.owner: DGCL (Direction Générale des Collectivités Locales), Ministry of Interior; offices attached to the communes
systems.tiers: about 2,200 local offices (1,503 principal commune offices, about 700 annexes) and 69 consular posts; no central repository
online service operating since 2012 for ordering copies of a birth registration act, delivered by courier post for 20 dirhams; the applicant must supply the act number, year and office
national electronic identity card for adults, 20 million issued, enrolled at about 100 CEDI centres with AFIS de-duplication; not electronically linked to the birth and death registers

note: Passages only. The diagnostic was prepared in July 2014 from a field visit of 23-28 June 2014, so facts are dated 2014-06 rather than to the 2016 publication. It also reports that the DGCL and the Ministry of Interior recognised the need to digitise the historical register, with cost, time and lack of consensus still to be overcome; MASSAR, RAMED and CNSS registers are described but lie outside the study's field.
